title: RCC structures-2
summary: Shear, columns, footings and prestressing share this subchapter. For shear, the crucial distinction is between tau_c (below which no stirrups are needed) and tau_c,max (above which the section must be enlarged, because stirrups cannot prevent web crushing). For columns, the minimum eccentricity rule and the tie spacing limits are the reliable marks. Prestressing questions almost always concern the losses and the pre- versus post-tensioning distinction.

sections.heading: Shear and torsion
sections.body:
**Nominal shear stress:**

> **τ_v = V_u / (b d)**

This is compared against two quite different limits, and confusing them is the standard error:

| Comparison | Meaning | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **τ_v ≤ τ_c/2** | Very low shear | Minimum stirrups may be omitted in slabs; still required in beams |
| **τ_v ≤ τ_c** | Concrete alone suffices | Provide **minimum** shear reinforcement |
| **τ_c < τ_v ≤ τ_c,max** | Stirrups required | **Design** shear reinforcement |
| **τ_v > τ_c,max** | **Web crushing** | **REDESIGN the section** — stirrups cannot help |

**τ_c** is the design shear strength of concrete alone (IS 456 Table 19), depending on the **grade** and on the **percentage of tension steel** — more steel gives a higher τ_c, because the steel restrains crack widening and preserves aggregate interlock across the crack.

**τ_c,max** (Table 20) is the absolute ceiling:

| Grade | M20 | M25 | M30 | M35 | M40+ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **τ_c,max** (N/mm²) | **2.8** | **3.1** | 3.5 | 3.7 | 4.0 |

**Why exceeding τ_c,max cannot be solved with more stirrups.** Beyond that stress the **concrete web crushes** in diagonal compression — the compressive struts between the diagonal cracks fail. Stirrups carry **tension** across the cracks; they do nothing to increase the compressive capacity of the strut. So the only remedies are a **larger section** or a **higher concrete grade**. A question offering "provide more stirrups" for τ_v > τ_c,max is offering a wrong answer that sounds reasonable.

**Shear reinforcement design:**

> **V_us = V_u − τ_c b d**   (the shear the stirrups must carry)
> **Vertical stirrups: V_us = 0.87 f_y A_sv d / s_v**

rearranged for spacing:

> **s_v = 0.87 f_y A_sv d / V_us**

**Minimum shear reinforcement (IS 456 cl. 26.5.1.6):**

> **A_sv/(b s_v) ≥ 0.4/(0.87 f_y)**

**Maximum spacing** is the least of **0.75 d**, **300 mm**, and the calculated value.

**Why a minimum is required even where τ_v < τ_c.** Shear failure in an unreinforced web is **sudden and brittle** — a diagonal tension crack opens and the beam fails without warning. Minimum stirrups hold the crack together, provide ductility, restrain the longitudinal bars against buckling, and hold the reinforcement cage in position during construction. The reasoning parallels the minimum flexural steel rule.

**Types of shear reinforcement:** **vertical stirrups** (the standard), **inclined stirrups** (more efficient, being closer to perpendicular to the crack), and **bent-up (inclined) bars** — though IS 456 requires that bent-up bars carry **not more than half** the total shear, the rest by stirrups, because bent-up bars are effective only over a limited length.

**Enhanced shear near supports.** IS 456 permits an increased τ_c within a distance **2d** of a support, because the load there is carried partly by direct **arch action** — a compression strut running from the load to the support — rather than by beam shear.

**Torsion.** IS 456 treats torsion by **equivalent** shear and moment rather than directly:

> **Equivalent shear V_e = V_u + 1.6 T_u/b**
> **Equivalent moment M_e1 = M_u + T_u(1 + D/b)/1.7**
> and if M_e1 exceeds M_u, a **second moment M_e2 = M_e1 − M_u** requires steel on the **other** face

The section is then designed for V_e and M_e as if there were no torsion. Torsion reinforcement consists of **closed stirrups** and **longitudinal bars at all corners** — an open U-stirrup is ineffective in torsion, because torsion requires a **closed loop** of shear flow around the section.

**Equilibrium versus compatibility torsion** is a distinction worth knowing: **equilibrium torsion** cannot be redistributed (a cantilevered canopy along a beam, where the beam must carry the twist or the canopy falls), while **compatibility torsion** arises only from the restraint of adjacent members and can largely be redistributed by cracking. IS 456 permits compatibility torsion to be neglected where the member can crack and rotate.

sections.heading: Columns
sections.body:
**Classification:**

| Basis | Types |
|---|---|
| **Slenderness** | **Short if L_e/D < 12** in both directions; otherwise **slender** |
| Loading | Axial, uniaxial bending, biaxial bending |
| Shape | Rectangular, square, circular, L, T |
| Reinforcement | **Tied** (lateral ties) or **spirally reinforced (helical)** |

**Short axially loaded column:**

> **P_u = 0.4 f_ck A_c + 0.67 f_y A_sc**

The **0.4** and **0.67** already include the partial safety factors and an allowance for the minimum eccentricity permitted without explicit calculation.

**Minimum eccentricity (IS 456 cl. 25.4):**

> **e_min = L/500 + D/30, but not less than 20 mm**

If the actual eccentricity does not exceed **0.05 D**, the formula above may be used. Beyond that, the column must be designed for **combined axial load and bending** using an **interaction (P–M) diagram** from SP 16.

**Why a minimum eccentricity exists:** no column is truly axially loaded. Construction tolerances, unequal beam loads, accidental moments and initial crookedness guarantee some eccentricity, and a formula assuming pure axial load would be unsafe. It is a recognition of reality rather than a safety factor.

**Reinforcement rules (IS 456 cl. 26.5.3):**

| Item | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Minimum longitudinal steel** | **0.8%** of the gross area |
| **Maximum** | **6%** (4% practical, to allow placing and lapping) |
| **Minimum number of bars** | **4** in a rectangular column, **6** in a circular one |
| **Minimum bar diameter** | **12 mm** |
| Maximum spacing of longitudinal bars | 300 mm along each face |
| **Minimum column dimension** | 200 mm (**300 mm** in a seismic frame, IS 13920) |

**Lateral ties** — the three-part rule that questions ask directly:

> **Diameter:** the **greater of ¼ of the largest longitudinal bar** and **6 mm**
> **Spacing:** the **least of** the **least lateral dimension** of the column, **16 × the smallest longitudinal bar diameter**, and **300 mm**

**What ties actually do**, which explains why they are not optional:

| Function | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Restrain longitudinal bars against buckling** | The primary purpose |
| **Confine the core concrete** | Raises its strength and, crucially, its **ductility** |
| Resist shear | Secondary |
| Hold the cage during construction | Practical |

The **confinement** function is why seismic detailing tightens the spacing so dramatically. **IS 13920** requires **special confining reinforcement** over a length of **2d** (or the larger of the member dimension, one sixth of the clear height, and 450 mm) at each end of a column, at a spacing not exceeding **the least of ¼ of the minimum member dimension, 6 × the smallest bar diameter, and 100 mm**.

That is a spacing of perhaps 75–100 mm against 300 mm in ordinary detailing — three to four times as much steel in the critical zone. It buys the **ductility** that the response reduction factor R assumed, and it is the difference between a column that hinges and survives and one that shatters.

**Spiral (helical) reinforcement** is **10% more efficient** than ties (IS 456 allows a 1.05 multiplier on the strength), because a continuous helix confines the core more effectively than discrete ties. Its condition is that the **volume of helical reinforcement per unit length** satisfies a minimum ratio related to the core and gross areas.

**Slender columns** must be designed for **additional moments** from the lateral deflection:

> **M_ax = P_u D (L_e/D)² / 2000**

and similarly about the other axis. The **effective length** depends on the end restraints and, in a frame, on the relative stiffnesses of the beams and columns at each joint (IS 456 Annex E).

**Biaxial bending** is checked by an interaction expression:

> **(M_ux/M_ux1)^{α_n} + (M_uy/M_uy1)^{α_n} ≤ 1**

with α_n between 1.0 and 2.0 depending on P_u/P_uz.

**Strong column–weak beam.** The governing principle of ductile frame design:

> **ΣM_column ≥ 1.4 ΣM_beam** at every joint (IS 13920)

The reason is that a **beam** hinge is a **local** failure the frame survives, while a **column** hinge causes **storey collapse**. The **soft or weak storey** — typically an open ground floor for parking or shops — is the classic violation, and it was a major cause of collapse in the 2015 Gorkha earthquake. Buildings with an open ground storey must be designed for **2.5 times** the storey forces obtained from ordinary analysis, or stiffened with shear walls or bracing.

sections.heading: Footings and retaining walls
sections.body:
**A footing is checked for four things**, and the order in which they govern is worth knowing:

| Check | Critical section | Usually governs |
|---|---|---|
| **Two-way (punching) shear** | Perimeter at **d/2** from the column face | **The thickness** |
| **One-way shear** | At **d** from the column face | Occasionally |
| **Bending** | **At the column face** | The reinforcement |
| **Development length / bearing** | — | Detailing |

**Punching shear** permissible stress:

> **τ_c = k_s × 0.25 √f_ck**,  with **k_s = (0.5 + β_c) ≤ 1.0**

where β_c is the ratio of the short to long side of the column. **Punching shear usually decides the footing depth**, which surprises candidates who size it for moment first.

**Area of the footing:**

> **A = total SERVICE load / net allowable bearing pressure**

Note the asymmetry: the **area** is found from **unfactored (service)** loads compared with the allowable soil pressure, but the **structural design** of the footing uses **factored** loads and the resulting **net upward pressure**. Mixing the two is a frequent error.

**Types:**

| Type | Use |
|---|---|
| **Isolated** | A single column |
| **Combined** | Two columns too close for separate footings; shaped so its **centroid coincides with the resultant** of the loads |
| **Strap (cantilever)** | A column at a **boundary**; the strap beam transfers moment and is designed for **bending only** |
| **Strip / continuous** | A load-bearing wall or a row of columns |
| **Raft** | Weak soil, large area; footings would otherwise cover more than half the plan |
| Pile cap | Transfers column load to a pile group |

**Reinforcement in a footing** runs in **both directions** in the bottom, with the **longer direction's steel placed lowest** where the moments differ — and for a rectangular footing IS 456 requires the steel in the **short** direction to be concentrated in a central band, because the pressure is not uniformly effective across the full length.

**Retaining walls.** The four stability checks and their minimum factors:

| Check | Minimum F |
|---|---|
| **Overturning** about the toe | **2.0** |
| **Sliding** along the base | **1.5** |
| **Bearing pressure** | **3.0** on ultimate capacity |
| **Overall slope failure** through the wall and foundation | **1.5** |

The **fourth is the one most often omitted**, and a wall perfectly stable in itself can ride down on a slip surface passing beneath it — which is exactly what happens on hill roads built on marginally stable slopes.

**No tension at the heel** requires the resultant within the **middle third**: **e ≤ B/6**.

**Structural design** of a cantilever retaining wall: the **stem** as a vertical cantilever carrying the earth pressure, the **heel slab** carrying the weight of soil above it downward, and the **toe slab** carrying the upward soil pressure. The critical sections are at the junctions with the base.

**Drainage is the single most important detail and the most neglected.** A wall designed for earth pressure alone and then allowed to accumulate water behind it can receive **two to three times** the design thrust, because hydrostatic pressure is **not reduced by K_a**. Most retaining wall failures are drainage failures.

The measures: **weep holes** (75–100 mm at 1–1.5 m centres), a **granular filter or drainage blanket** behind the wall, a **longitudinal perforated drain** at the base, a **geotextile filter** to stop fines migrating, and **surface sealing at the crest** to prevent infiltration in the first place. **Free-draining granular backfill** is specified for the same reason, and clay is a poor choice because it holds water and develops a tension crack that fills with it.

**Compaction of the backfill** needs care in both directions: too little and the fill subsides; too much and **compaction-induced lateral pressure** from heavy rollers working close to the wall can exceed the at-rest value and push it forward. Light plant is used within about 1 m of the wall.

**Water tanks** are the other common water-retaining structure, and their design differs in one important respect: **crack control governs**, not strength. IS 3370 limits the permissible **steel stress** to keep crack widths small — around **115–150 N/mm²** for direct tension — which is far below 0.87 f_y. That means water-retaining structures carry considerably more steel than strength alone would require, and it is why the working stress method persisted for them long after limit state design took over elsewhere.

sections.heading: Prestressed concrete
sections.body:
**The idea.** Concrete is strong in compression and weak in tension. **Prestressing** introduces a permanent compression that the service loads must first overcome before any tension appears — so the **whole section remains uncracked and effective**, instead of only the compression zone.

**Consequences of that**, which are the advantages:

| Advantage | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Full section effective** | No cracked tension zone, so the section is stiffer for the same size |
| **Longer spans, shallower members** | Higher efficiency |
| **No cracking under service load** | Better **durability** — no route for water and chloride to the steel |
| Lighter members, less dead load | — |
| Deflection can be **cambered out** | The prestress acts against the load |
| Better **fatigue** and shear performance | Stress range is reduced |

Against which: **high-strength materials are essential**, the workmanship and supervision must be better, specialised equipment is needed, and the **losses** must be predicted accurately.

**High-strength materials are not optional but necessary.** Prestressing steel is stressed to about **1400–1600 N/mm²**, so ordinary mild steel could not be used — its yield strength is a sixth of that. And concrete must be high grade (**M30 minimum for post-tensioned, M40 for pre-tensioned**, IS 1343) both to resist the large compression at the anchorage and to reduce the **creep and shrinkage** that cause losses.

**Pre-tensioning versus post-tensioning** — the distinction examined every time:

| | **Pre-tensioning** | **Post-tensioning** |
|---|---|---|
| Sequence | Steel stressed **BEFORE** casting | Steel stressed **AFTER** concrete hardens |
| Force transferred by | **BOND** between steel and concrete | **ANCHORAGES** at the ends |
| Tendon profile | **Straight** (or deflected with hold-downs) | **Curved** — can follow the moment diagram |
| Suits | **Factory precast**, repetitive units — sleepers, poles, planks, beams | **Cast in situ**, large members, bridges, long spans |
| Losses | **Higher** — full elastic shortening, plus more creep and shrinkage | Lower; no friction loss in the pre-tensioned case but friction in ducts here |
| Equipment | Casting bed with abutments | Jacks, ducts, anchorages, grouting |

The **curved tendon profile** is post-tensioning's structural advantage: a tendon following the shape of the bending moment diagram produces an upward load that opposes the applied load at every section, which is the ideal arrangement. Pre-tensioned straight tendons can only approximate it.

**Losses of prestress** — the most examined item, and they must be listed with their causes:

| Loss | Cause | Pre-tensioning | Post-tensioning |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Elastic shortening of concrete** | The concrete shortens as the force is applied | **Full** loss | Only for tendons stressed **before** later ones |
| **Creep of concrete** | Sustained compression | Higher | Lower |
| **Shrinkage of concrete** | Drying | Higher (concrete is younger at transfer) | Lower |
| **Relaxation of steel** | Steel loses stress at constant strain | Both | Both |
| **Friction** | Tendon rubbing in the duct — **wobble and curvature** | Not applicable | **Applies** |
| **Anchorage slip (draw-in)** | Wedges seating | Small | **Applies** |

**Total losses are typically 15–25%** of the initial prestress, and are **higher in pre-tensioning** — chiefly because the full elastic shortening occurs and because the concrete is younger and therefore shrinks and creeps more after transfer.

**Methods of analysis.** Three equivalent viewpoints, and being able to switch between them is the real skill:

1. **Stress concept** — superpose the stresses from prestress and from load: **σ = P/A ± Pe/Z ± M/Z**. The most direct for checking permissible stresses.
2. **Strength concept** — treat it as a section with an internal couple, as in reinforced concrete. Used at the ultimate limit state.
3. **Load balancing** — the curved tendon exerts an **equivalent upward UDL** of **8Pe/L²** on the concrete, which can be made to balance the applied load exactly. The most illuminating for design, because it shows immediately what profile is needed.

**Types of prestressing:**

| Type | Character |
|---|---|
| **Full prestressing** | **No tension** permitted under service load |
| **Partial prestressing** | Limited tension and controlled cracking permitted — more economical |
| **Circular prestressing** | Wires wound around **circular tanks, pipes, silos** — a direct application of hoop tension |
| Linear prestressing | Beams, slabs, girders |

**Circular prestressing** is worth noting for water supply: a prestressed concrete tank or pipe is put into permanent hoop compression by winding tensioned wire around it, so the internal water pressure never puts the concrete into tension. It is why prestressed concrete pipes can carry substantial pressure.

**Where prestressing is used in Nepal:** **bridge girders** (post-tensioned I and box girders are now standard for medium spans), **precast poles and sleepers**, water tanks, and long-span roofs. Its adoption has been driven by the same logic as everywhere else — for a given span, a prestressed member is shallower and lighter, which matters most where transport to site is difficult.

formulas.label: Nominal shear stress and its two limits
formulas.expression: τ_v = V_u/(bd) ;   τ_v ≤ τ_c → minimum stirrups ;   τ_v > τ_c,max → REDESIGN the section
formulas.note: τ_c,max = 2.8 (M20), 3.1 (M25). Beyond it the web crushes in diagonal compression; stirrups cannot help.

formulas.label: Shear reinforcement
formulas.expression: V_us = V_u − τ_c b d ;   s_v = 0.87 f_y A_sv d / V_us
formulas.note: Minimum A_sv/(b s_v) ≥ 0.4/(0.87 f_y). Maximum spacing least of 0.75d, 300 mm.

formulas.label: Torsion as equivalent shear and moment
formulas.note: Requires CLOSED stirrups — an open U-stirrup is ineffective in torsion.

formulas.label: Short axially loaded column
formulas.note: Valid while e ≤ 0.05D. Short means L_e/D < 12 in both directions.

formulas.label: Minimum eccentricity
formulas.expression: e_min = L/500 + D/30, not less than 20 mm
formulas.note: No column is truly axial. Beyond 0.05D use a P–M interaction diagram.

formulas.label: Column ties
formulas.expression: diameter ≥ greater of ¼ largest bar and 6 mm ;  spacing ≤ least of (least lateral dimension, 16 × smallest bar, 300 mm)
formulas.note: IS 13920 tightens this to the least of ¼ min dimension, 6 × smallest bar, and 100 mm in end zones.

formulas.label: Slender column additional moment
formulas.note: Applied about each axis. Effective length from IS 456 Annex E for frames.

formulas.label: Punching shear in a footing
formulas.expression: τ_v on a perimeter at d/2 from the column face ≤ k_s × 0.25√f_ck,  k_s = (0.5 + β_c) ≤ 1.0
formulas.note: Usually governs the footing THICKNESS. Area of footing from SERVICE loads, design from FACTORED loads.

formulas.label: Strong column–weak beam
formulas.note: A beam hinge is survivable; a column hinge causes storey collapse. Open ground storey: design for 2.5× forces.

formulas.label: Prestress — stress and load balancing concepts
formulas.expression: σ = P/A ± Pe/Z ± M/Z ;   equivalent upward UDL from a parabolic tendon = 8Pe/L²
formulas.note: Total losses typically 15–25%, HIGHER in pre-tensioning because full elastic shortening occurs.
